instructions:
You are judging translations of one English original into Australian English vernacular. The candidates
are anonymous (A, B, C ...) and in random order; they may come from a rule engine, a language model or a
person. Judge each against the original and against the brief: the level of Aussie (1 tourist: a light
touch; 5 swaggie: a full pub yarn) and the vulgarity allowed (0 nan: no swearing; 1 dad: bloody, bugger,
bastard; 2 uncle-bob: piss, arse, fuck; 3 tradie: the c-word too). A candidate is neither better nor worse
for being longer, or for using more slang than the brief asks for.

Each criterion measures one thing, so one weakness costs a candidate once. How much Aussie there is, against
the brief, is register; how natural the Aussie that is there sounds is authenticity. A text left largely
untranslated scores low on register, and is judged on authenticity, tone and essence by what it does say.
The change of voice the brief asks for (a press release told as a yarn) is not a loss of tone. An aside that
reacts to or elaborates something in the original is colour; a new fact, event or claim is invented, and
counts against meaning.

For each candidate and each criterion, write the evidence first: what you saw, quoting the candidate
verbatim in double quotes. Then give the score. Use the anchors; a 2 or a 4 sits between them. Then list
the candidate's specific problems, each with a verbatim quote from the candidate, the original passage it
renders (empty when the line is added and renders nothing), a severity (critical: changes or loses meaning
that matters; major: wrong sense, wrong register, or something an Australian would wince at; minor: a
weaker choice), and why. A problem that runs through the whole text is listed once, with one
representative quote. Last, rank the candidates on each comparison criterion and overall: a list of tiers,
best first, each tier the candidates you can't separate (most tiers hold one).

CRITERIA
- meaning: Does it say everything the original says, and nothing that changes it?
    1: Events, facts or claims lost or changed; a reader would come away with a different story.
    3: The gist survives, but some details are lost, changed or invented.
    5: Every point survives; additions are colour that hangs off something in the original.
- sense: Does every Aussie term carry the original's sense in its context?
    1: Several terms took the wrong sense ("the latest version" as gossip, "terrible" as rude).
    3: One or two terms took the wrong sense, or strain to fit.
    5: Every term fits its context exactly.
- authenticity: Would an Australian hear the Aussie it uses as natural, not a tourist's pastiche (however much or little there is)?
    1: Stage-Australian; stock phrases bolted on; US or British forms left in.
    3: Mostly natural, with some stock or forced lines.
    5: Sounds like a real Australian talking; idiom used the way locals use it.
- register: Is it as Aussie, and as rude, as the brief asked, no more and no less?
    1: Far off the brief (a level-1 brief told as a pub yarn, or swearing past the vulgarity allowed).
    3: Somewhat off: noticeably heavier or lighter than asked.
    5: Exactly the weight the brief asked for.
- tone: Does it keep the original's tone under the slang (solemn stays solemn, a joke stays a joke)? (also ranked across candidates)
    1: The tone is lost or inverted (a eulogy played for laughs, a warning made flippant).
    3: The tone wobbles in places.
    5: The original's tone comes through whole.
- flow: Does it read smoothly aloud, without pile-ups, clunky joins or repetition? (also ranked across candidates)
    1: Hard to read; stacked synonyms, broken grammar, jarring joins.
    3: Readable, with some clunky stretches.
    5: Reads like it was written that way.
- variety: Does it vary its slang, openers and tags, rather than leaning on a few? (also ranked across candidates)
    1: The same few terms or tics over and over.
    3: Some repetition a reader would notice.
    5: Varied throughout, with nothing leaned on.
- essence: Leaving aside how much it is retold (that is register), does it keep what the original is about and what makes it itself, its point, shape and character? (also ranked across candidates)
    1: Could be a different text; what made the original distinctive is gone.
    3: Recognisably the original, but flattened.
    5: Unmistakably the original, retold.

## Introduction

GitHub flow is a lightweight, branch-based workflow. The GitHub flow is useful for everyone, not just developers. For example, here at GitHub, we use GitHub flow for our [site policy](https://github.com/github/site-policy), [documentation](https://github.com/github/docs), and [roadmap](https://github.com/github/roadmap).

## Prerequisites

To follow GitHub flow, you will need a GitHub account and a repository. For information on how to create an account, see [Creating an account on GitHub](/en/account-and-profile/how-tos/account-management/creating-an-account-on-github). For information on how to create a repository, see [Quickstart for repositories](/en/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/quickstart-for-repositories). For information on how to find an existing repository to contribute to, see [Finding ways to contribute to open source on GitHub](/en/get-started/exploring-projects-on-github/finding-ways-to-contribute-to-open-source-on-github).

## Following GitHub flow

> \[!TIP]
> You can complete all steps of GitHub flow through the GitHub web interface, command line and [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com), or [GitHub Desktop](/en/desktop). For more information about the tools you can use to connect to GitHub, see [Connecting to GitHub](/en/get-started/using-github/connecting-to-github).

### Create a branch

Create a branch in your repository. A short, descriptive branch name enables your collaborators to see ongoing work at a glance. For example, `increase-test-timeout` or `add-code-of-conduct`. For more information, see [Managing branches within your repository](/en/pull-requests/how-tos/commit-changes/managing-branches-within-your-repository).

By creating a branch, you create a space to work without affecting the default branch. Additionally, you give collaborators a chance to review your work.

### Make changes

On your branch, make any desired changes to the repository. For more information, see [Creating new files](/en/repositories/working-with-files/managing-files/creating-new-files), [Editing files](/en/repositories/working-with-files/managing-files/editing-files), [Renaming a file](/en/repositories/working-with-files/managing-files/renaming-a-file), [Moving a file to a new location](/en/repositories/working-with-files/managing-files/moving-a-file-to-a-new-location), or [Deleting files in a repository](/en/repositories/working-with-files/managing-files/deleting-files-in-a-repository).

Your branch is a safe place to make changes. If you make a mistake, you can revert your changes or push additional changes to fix the mistake. Your changes will not end up on the default branch until you merge your branch.

Commit and push your changes to your branch. Give each commit a descriptive message to help you and future contributors understand what changes the commit contains. For example, `fix typo` or `increase rate limit`.

Ideally, each commit contains an isolated, complete change. This makes it easy to revert your changes if you decide to take a different approach. For example, if you want to rename a variable and add some tests, put the variable rename in one commit and the tests in another commit. Later, if you want to keep the tests but revert the variable rename, you can revert the specific commit that contained the variable rename. If you put the variable rename and tests in the same commit or spread the variable rename across multiple commits, you would spend more effort reverting your changes.

By committing and pushing your changes, you back up your work to remote storage. This means that you can access your work from any device. It also means that your collaborators can see your work, answer questions, and make suggestions or contributions.

Continue to make, commit, and push changes to your branch until you are ready to ask for feedback.

## Introduction

GitHub flow is a lightweight, branch-based workflow. The GitHub flow is useful for every man and his dog, not just developers. For example, here at GitHub, we use GitHub flow for our [site policy](https://github.com/github/site-policy), [documentation](https://github.com/github/docs), and [roadmap](https://github.com/github/roadmap).

## Prerequisites

To follow GitHub flow, you'll need a GitHub account and a repository. For information on how to create an account, see [Creating an account on GitHub](/en/account-and-profile/how-tos/account-management/creating-an-account-on-github). For information on how to create a repository, see [Quickstart for repositories](/en/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/quickstart-for-repositories). For information on how to find an existing repository to contribute to, see [Findin' ways to contribute to open source on GitHub](/en/get-started/exploring-projects-on-github/finding-ways-to-contribute-to-open-source-on-github).

## Following GitHub flow

> \[!TIP]
> Ya can complete all steps of GitHub flow through the GitHub web interface, command line and [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com), or [GitHub Desktop](/en/desktop). For more information about the tools you can use to connect to GitHub, see [Connecting to GitHub](/en/get-started/using-github/connecting-to-github).

### Create a branch

Create a branch in yer repository. A short, descriptive branch name enables yer collaborators to see ongoing work at a squiz. For example, `increase-test-timeout` or `add-code-of-conduct`. For more information, see [Managing branches within yer repository](/en/pull-requests/how-tos/commit-changes/managing-branches-within-your-repository).

By creating a branch, ya create a space to work without affectin' the default branch. Additionally, ya give collaborators a chance to review yer work.

### Make changes

On yer branch, make any desired changes to the repository. For more information, see [Creating brand-spankin'-new files](/en/repositories/working-with-files/managing-files/creating-new-files), [Editing files](/en/repositories/working-with-files/managing-files/editing-files), [Renamin' a file](/en/repositories/working-with-files/managing-files/renaming-a-file), [Moving a file to a brand-spankin'-new location](/en/repositories/working-with-files/managing-files/moving-a-file-to-a-new-location), or [Deleting files in a repository](/en/repositories/working-with-files/managing-files/deleting-files-in-a-repository).

Your branch is a safe place to make changes. If you make a mistake, ya can revert your changes or push additional changes to fix the mistake. Yer changes won't end up on the default branch until ya merge yer branch.

Commit and push yer changes to yer branch. Give each commit a descriptive message to help ya and future contributors understand what changes the commit contains. For example, `fix typo` or `increase rate limit`.

Ideally, each commit contains an isolated, complete change. This makes it easy to revert your changes if you decide to take a different approach. For example, if ya wanna rename a variable and add some tests, put the variable rename in one commit'n the tests in another commit. Later, if ya want to keep the tests but revert the variable rename, ya can revert the specific commit that contained the variable rename. If ya put the variable rename and tests in the same commit or spread the variable rename across multiple commits, ya would spend more effort reverting yer changes.

By committin''n pushin' yer changes, you back up yer work to remote storage. This means that you can access yer work from any device. It also means that yer collaborators can see yer work, answer questions, and make suggestions or contributions.

Continue to make, commit, and push changes to yer branch until yer ready to ask for feedback.
